narrative:
**HEADLINE**
Overall macro risk remains High, with no intraday level changes; private credit opacity and geopolitical supply-chain vulnerabilities dominate the risk surface.

**STORIES WITH CHANGES**
No stories shifted risk bands today.

**STANDING ELEVATED OR HIGH RISKS**
• **Private credit's opaque expansion** (High) – largest absolute level at 8; minimal transparency into collateral quality and redemption pressures poses systemic spillover risk.
• **Japan fiscal / JGB / carry trade** (High) – persistent funding and unwind vulnerability.
• **AI power & the grid bottleneck** (High) – infrastructure capacity constraints threaten build-out continuity.
• **Food & fertilizer fragility** (High) – supply-chain and geopolitical exposure.
• **Sea lanes & undersea cables** (High) – chokepoint risk to global data and trade flows.
• **Critical minerals as a weapon** (High) – geopolitical leverage over energy and tech transition.
• **Treasury basis trade (hidden leverage)** (Elevated) – embedded leverage in repo markets.
• **Developing-world debt crisis** (Elevated) – refinancing pressure amid rate environment.
• **China's price spillover** (Elevated) – deflationary transmission risk.
• **AI build-out circular financing** (Elevated) – concentration of funding sources.

**WATCH CLOSEST**
Private credit's opacity (level 8) remains the single highest-risk vector given systemic interconnection and limited visibility into forced asset sales.

stories.name: Treasury basis trade (hidden leverage)

indicators.label: SOFR minus EFFR (%)
MOVE index (Treasury volatility)
SEC central clearing on track (0 ok / 1 slipping / 2 delayed)

stories.summary: Hedge funds run a highly leveraged arbitrage between Treasury cash bonds and futures. It is a major source of liquidity, but a spike in funding costs or Treasury volatility can force rapid unwinds, as briefly happened in March 2020 and again in 2025.

stories.name: Japan fiscal / JGB / carry trade

indicators.label: USD/JPY (yen strengthening = lower = risk)
30-year JGB yield (%)
Takaichi plan financing clarity (0 ok / 1 unclear / 2 disorderly)

stories.summary: Decades of near-zero rates made Japan the funding leg of a vast global carry trade. As the BoJ normalizes and JGB yields rise, fiscal financing gets harder and carry unwinds can transmit stress worldwide - the August 2024 mini-crash was a preview.

stories.name: Private credit's opaque expansion

indicators.label: US high-yield OAS (%, ≈310bps)
Direct-lending default rate (%, Fitch incl. distressed exchanges)
Large-fund redemption gates (0 none / 1 isolated / 2 widespread)

stories.summary: Lending has migrated from banks to lightly regulated private-credit funds, where assets are marked infrequently and leverage is opaque. Defaults are rising from a low base; the risk is that losses surface suddenly rather than being visible in real time.

stories.name: Developing-world debt crisis

indicators.label: Broad US dollar index (FRED DTWEXBGS)
US 10y real yield (TIPS, %)
New IMF programs / missed coupons (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 cluster)

stories.summary: A strong dollar, high real rates, and heavy foreign-currency debt loads leave many developing economies vulnerable to a sudden stop. A cluster of sovereign defaults or new IMF programs would signal the slow-burn crisis turning acute.

stories.name: China's price spillover (deflation or cost-push)

indicators.label: China PPI YoY (%) - large swing either way is worse
USD/CNY (yuan depreciation = higher = risk)
New tariff/anti-dumping actions (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 escalating)

stories.summary: China's factory-gate prices spill into global goods markets in BOTH directions: years of PPI deflation exported disinflation and squeezed competitors, while a sharp 2026 reversal to positive PPI (energy/commodity cost-push) now exports input-cost pressure. Either large swing is destabilising; the indicator is scored on the size of the move, not its sign.

stories.name: Critical minerals as a weapon

indicators.label: Rare-earth export license flow (0 flowing / 1 slowing / 2 frozen)
Nov-2025 pause status (0 extended / 1 expiring / 2 lapsed)
US domestic RE producer blacklist (0 none / 1 entity-specific ban / 2 sector-wide ban)
Ex-China heavy rare-earth price premium (x China)

stories.summary: China dominates the mining and especially the processing of rare earths and critical minerals, and has shown willingness to use export licensing as leverage. Supply chains for magnets and defense inputs have little near-term substitute.

stories.name: Stablecoins & Treasury demand

indicators.label: Largest stablecoin max peg deviation (%)
Total USD stablecoin supply ($bn)
GENIUS implementation friction (0 smooth / 1 gaps / 2 problems)

stories.summary: Dollar stablecoins have become sizeable holders of short-term Treasuries, linking crypto plumbing to the funding market. A large redemption wave could force rapid T-bill selling; the GENIUS Act's implementation is the key regulatory variable.

stories.name: AI build-out circular financing

indicators.label: US investment-grade OAS (%) - big-issuer proxy
AI capex-vs-revenue gap concern (0 closing / 1 wide / 2 widening fast)
GPU-backed debt refinancing stress (0 none / 1 signs / 2 acute)

stories.summary: AI infrastructure spending vastly exceeds current AI revenue, increasingly financed with debt and circular vendor arrangements. If monetization disappoints or GPU-backed financing strains, the capex cycle could reverse sharply.

stories.name: CRE maturity wall / regional banks

indicators.label: CMBS office delinquency rate (%)
Regional-bank CRE stress (0 calm / 1 isolated / 2 cluster)

stories.summary: A wall of commercial real-estate loans - especially office - matures into higher rates and lower valuations, concentrated at regional banks. Rising delinquencies and 'extend and pretend' practices defer, rather than resolve, the losses.

stories.name: France / eurozone fragility

indicators.label: OAT-Bund 10y spread (%)
Govt stability (0 stable / 1 fragile / 2 collapse-or-snap-election)
Rating action (0 stable / 1 negative outlook / 2 downgrade)

stories.summary: France combines a wide deficit, a fragmented parliament, and recurring budget standoffs, widening its spread over Germany. Political instability or a rating downgrade would test eurozone cohesion at its second-largest economy.

stories.name: Hidden consumer debt

indicators.label: Subprime auto 60+ day delinquency (%)
US unemployment rate (%)
BNPL delinquency trend (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 spiking)

stories.summary: Beneath headline figures, subprime auto and buy-now-pay-later delinquencies are climbing, and the labor market is the swing factor. A rise in unemployment would convert stretched-but-current borrowers into defaults quickly.

stories.name: Gold / de-dollarization

indicators.label: Gold price (USD/oz)
USD share of FX reserves (%, IMF COFER)
Reserve-weaponization / settlement shift (0 none / 1 talk / 2 action)

stories.summary: Central banks are accumulating gold and building non-dollar settlement arrangements at the margin. It is a slow erosion rather than a sudden shift, but reserve 'weaponization' events can accelerate diversification away from the dollar.

stories.name: Insurance retreat

indicators.label: Insurer non-renewals / exits (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 accelerating)
US single-family mortgage delinquency (%, FRED DRSFRMACBS)
Catastrophe-loss pressure (0 normal / 1 elevated / 2 severe season)

stories.summary: Insurers are retreating from climate-exposed markets through non-renewals and exits, shifting risk onto homeowners and state backstops. Severe catastrophe seasons strain the system and feed into housing and mortgage stress.

stories.name: Pensions / demographics

indicators.label: Social Security / pension reform shock (0 none / 1 debate / 2 cuts)
Pension-fund leverage event, UK-2022 type (0 none / 1 stress / 2 blowup)
Large public-pension funded ratio (%)

stories.summary: Aging demographics and underfunded public pensions create slow fiscal pressure, while leveraged liability-driven strategies can blow up fast - as the UK gilt/LDI crisis showed in 2022. Benefit-reform fights are the political pressure valve.

stories.name: AI power & the grid bottleneck

indicators.label: Grid interconnection wait (months)
Data-center moratoria / backlash (0 none / 1 spreading / 2 widespread)
AI power-demand pressure (0 easing / 1 tight / 2 acute)

stories.summary: Data-center electricity demand is colliding with multi-year grid interconnection queues and slow capacity additions. Whether this is an acute shortfall or eases depends on the pace of AI build-out versus new supply - forecasts diverge widely.

stories.name: Copper & the electrification deficit

indicators.label: Copper price (USD/lb, COMEX HG=F)
Major mine disruptions (0 none / 1 some / 2 cluster)
Deficit timing (0 surplus / 1 balanced / 2 deficit)

stories.summary: Electrification and AI infrastructure point to structural copper deficits as demand outruns new mine supply, which takes a decade to build. Price is the live signal; mine disruptions and inventory draws would confirm tightening.

stories.name: Water - the underpriced input

indicators.label: Drought in a chip/farm hub (0 none / 1 emerging / 2 acute)
Key reservoir / basin stress (0 normal / 1 low / 2 critical)
Transboundary water dispute escalation (0 calm / 1 tense / 2 crisis)

stories.summary: Water is systematically underpriced yet essential to chip fabrication, agriculture, and power. Droughts in key hubs (Taiwan's fabs, major farming regions) and transboundary disputes can disrupt supply chains in ways markets rarely price in advance.

stories.name: Food & fertilizer fragility

indicators.label: Food-price trend (0 falling / 1 elevated / 2 spiking)
China fertilizer export curbs (0 lifted / 1 in place / 2 tightened)
Hormuz/Gulf disruption to fertilizer inputs (0 clear / 1 disrupted / 2 cut)

stories.summary: Food security depends on concentrated fertilizer supply chains - potash, phosphate, and gas-derived nitrogen - exposed to export curbs and shipping chokepoints. Curbs or input shocks feed through to prices with a lag.

stories.name: The lithography (ASML) chokepoint

indicators.label: Taiwan / cross-strait tension (0 calm / 1 elevated / 2 crisis)
Export-control escalation (0 stable / 1 tightening / 2 retaliation)
Single-point concentration (0 easing / 1 high / 2 extreme)

stories.summary: ASML is the sole maker of EUV lithography machines, with Zeiss the sole optics supplier - a single point of failure for advanced chips. Export controls, retaliation, or any disruption to this chain would ripple across the entire tech economy.

stories.name: Sea lanes & undersea cables

indicators.label: Hormuz/Red Sea status (0 open / 1 contested / 2 closed)
WTI crude oil (USD/bbl, CL=F)
Undersea cable incidents (0 none / 1 threatened / 2 cut)

stories.summary: A few maritime chokepoints and undersea cables carry most global trade and data. The 2026 Hormuz/Red Sea disruptions showed how quickly closures spike energy and shipping costs; cable cuts are a parallel, under-watched vulnerability.

stories.name: Clearinghouses (financial chokepoint)

indicators.label: Equity volatility (VIX)
Treasury volatility (MOVE)
Treasury-clearing rollout stress (0 smooth / 1 friction / 2 problems)

stories.summary: Central counterparties now concentrate the system's risk by design, and Treasury central-clearing mandates will route more activity through them. In a volatility spike, procyclical margin calls can amplify stress - they are a systemic single point of failure.

items.label: GENIUS implementation friction (0 smooth / 1 gaps / 2 problems)
items.rationale: The rubric scores 2 for 'deadline missed without final rules.' The July 18, 2026 statutory deadline passed with zero final rules published across all primary regulators (OCC, FDIC, NCUA, Federal Reserve, Treasury); all packages remain at NPRM stage with some comment periods still running into August 2026, satisfying the rubric's 'deadline missed without final rules' criterion unambiguously. The GENIUS Act's 18-month effective-date backstop (Jan 18, 2027) now governs, further confirming the rulemaking failure.
items.fact: U.S. regulators missed the GENIUS Act statutory July 18, 2026 rulemaking deadline without issuing any final rules. As of that date, principal rule packages from the OCC, FDIC, NCUA, and Treasury remained Notices of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRMs); several comment periods remained open past the deadline (e.g., a joint customer-identification rule open until Aug. 21, an FDIC AML proposal open until Aug. 4). No final rules had been published as of late August 2026. Source: The Block, July 18 2026 (https://www.theblock.co/news/regulation/2026-07-18-us-regulators-miss-genius-acts-one-year-deadline-for-final-stablecoin-rules-408843); crypto.news, ~Aug 2026 (https://crypto.news/genius-act-missed-deadline-regulators-writing-rules/); tech-insider.org, ~July 24 2026 (https://tech-insider.org/genius-act-stablecoin-law/).

dissent.view: The missed deadline does not void the GENIUS Act or its Jan. 18, 2027 effective date; agencies are continuing to finalize rules on their own post-deadline timeline, and no court stay or compliance-failure event has occurred—some observers characterise this as a delay rather than a structural breakdown.

items.label: Large-fund redemption gates (0 none / 1 isolated / 2 widespread)
items.rationale: 10 of 16 BDCs in the Fitch sample breached quarterly caps simultaneously in Q2 2026, with at least 4 named funds - including BCRED ($79B) alone exceeding the $100B combined AUM threshold - clearly meeting the WIDESPREAD criterion of >=3 largest funds gating in the same quarter with combined AUM well above $100B. No corroborating rate or repo stress is required by rubric for structural cap breaches, but MOVE index elevation and asset-manager equity drawdowns corroborate systemic pressure.
items.fact: Fitch Ratings data (cited by multiple sources, Aug 2026): 10 of 16 tracked non-traded BDCs breached quarterly redemption caps in Q2 2026. Named funds simultaneously gated in Q2: Blackstone BCRED (~$79B AUM, ~10% requests vs 5% cap), Apollo Debt Solutions BDC (~16.8% requests vs 5% cap), Morgan Stanley North Haven Private Income Fund ($7B, 11.6% vs 5% cap), Cliffwater CCLFX (~$31B, 17% vs 5% cap). Blue Owl OBDC II ($1.6B) permanently closed gates. Robert A. Stanger & Co. puts Q2 repurchase requests at 12.4% of NAV - highest on record - with only 38% fulfilled and ~$9.6B backlog. (Sources: ecmsource.com citing WSJ/Bloomberg/CNBC June 2026; angelinvestorsnetwork.com citing Fitch, Aug 2026; tradingmarketsignals.com citing Stanger, Aug 17 2026)

dissent.view: CLA Wealth Advisors (Mar 2026) and CAIA (Apr 2026) characterise the episode as funds 'operating as designed' within contractual limits - not a gating crisis but structural mechanics functioning normally; they note caps are contractual features, not emergency restrictions.
iCapital argues credit fundamentals remain sound and the redemption process is 'orderly', distinguishing elevated requests from systemic distress.

items.label: Takaichi plan financing clarity (0 ok / 1 unclear / 2 disorderly)
items.rationale: The 10-year yield has risen roughly +80 bps from ~2.1% in March to ~3.0% on fiscal-concern news, far exceeding the 25 bps UNCLEAR threshold and approaching the 50 bps DISORDERLY threshold; however, all recent auctions have cleared well above BTC 2 (30y BTC 3.79) with no failed auction or emergency BOJ operation, so the rubric's DISORDERLY criterion (failed auction or >50 bps spike in a single fiscal-news event) is not cleanly met, keeping the reading at UNCLEAR (1).
items.fact: Japan's 10-year JGB yield reached 3.000% on 1 September 2026 — its highest since 1996 — triggered by a record ¥143 trillion in FY2027 budget requests submitted on 31 August, with the Takaichi government declining to set spending ceilings for a new investment/national-security category; the 10y yield stood at ~2.9% on 7 September. However, the 30-year JGB auction on 3 September cleared with a bid-to-cover of 3.79 vs. a 12-month average of 3.52 (Bloomberg, 3 Sept 2026), and the 10-year auction on 1 September also reportedly cleared with robust demand (Universal Asset Owners, 1 Sept 2026). No emergency BOJ operation or failed auction (BTC <2) has been reported.

dissent.view: Universal Asset Owners / The Probability Desk (1 Sept 2026) characterises the 3% print as a 'term-premium event, not a fiscal crisis,' noting the same-day 10y auction cleared with robust demand, suggesting conditions are closer to 0 than 1.

items.label: Treasury-clearing rollout stress (0 smooth / 1 friction / 2 problems)
items.rationale: The rubric scores 1=FRICTION when there is a documentation backlog or pending exemptive relief: both conditions are confirmed simultaneously — TBAC/TBACC cite ongoing legal-agreement backlogs and multiple SEC exemptive-relief requests (inter-affiliate, cross-border, omnibus margin) remain open as of early September 2026. No deadline extension (which would trigger score 2) has been announced, and DTCC reports strong infrastructure progress with 79% account readiness, ruling out score 0. [vintage guard: new read is 2026-08-07 data but the prior applied value was 2026-08 data; kept the newer vintage]
items.fact: DTCC/FICC survey (July 27, 2026) found >$1.2T of Treasury cash activity already clearing at FICC with ~$300-400B still to onboard, and 79% of GSD netting members have account setups in place; simultaneously, as of Aug 7, 2026, the SEC had multiple pending exemptive-relief requests unresolved (SIFMA inter-affiliate, IIB cross-border, and 15c3-3 omnibus-margin relief with comment period closing Aug 31, 2026), and TBAC Q2 2026 (May 2026) identified documentation/legal-agreement backlogs as the 'largest challenge.' No deadline extension has been announced. Sources: DTCC/Finadium July 27 2026 (https://finadium.com/ficc-survey-shows-ust-clearing-at-scale-ahead-of-sec-deadline/); SEC Commissioner Uyeda statement Aug 7 2026 (https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/speeches-statements/uyeda-statement-update-secs-work-toward-treasury-clearing-implementation-080726-update-secs-work-toward-treasury-clearing-implementation-august-2026); TBAC Charge Q2 2026 May 2026 (https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/221/TBACCharge1Q22026.pdf).

dissent.view: DTCC president Brian Steele stated the industry is 'well positioned for the Treasury cash clearing deadline on December 31, 2026,' suggesting closer to SMOOTH (0); $1.2T already clearing indicates substantial completion.

items.label: AI capex-vs-revenue gap concern (0 closing / 1 wide / 2 widening fast)
items.rationale: Capex growth (~77% YoY) materially exceeds AI-cloud revenue growth rates (~37-82% YoY), keeping the gap WIDE; however, AI-attributable revenues are accelerating QoQ across all three major cloud segments - not decelerating - which disqualifies the WIDENING FAST (2) classification and firmly places this at rubric level 1.
items.fact: Four hyperscalers (Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft) raised 2026 capex guidance to ~$725-760B (+77% YoY from ~$410B in 2025), with Amazon lifting to ~$220B and Alphabet to $195-205B at Q2 earnings. AI-attributable cloud revenue in Q2 2026 accelerated QoQ: Google Cloud +82% YoY to $24.8B (up from +63% in Q1), Azure +43% YoY (up from +40% in FY Q2), AWS +37% YoY to $42.23B; Microsoft AI annualized run rate $37B +123% YoY. Sources: Microsoft 8-K Jul 29 2026 (SEC); saasrise.com/news Aug 2026; valueaddvc.com Aug 2026; Financial Times via Yahoo Finance Apr 30 2026.

dissent.view: Sequoia Capital (David Cahn, 2025 estimate) put the annual gap between AI infrastructure spend and AI ecosystem revenue at ~$600B; no 2026 update confirms narrowing - suggesting the gap may be worse than headline cloud growth rates imply when non-hyperscaler AI revenue is included

Moody's May 2026 forecast revision flagged explicit credit risk if 'strong profit growth from AI investments fails to materialise', implying ratings-agency concern that current revenue trajectory may not suffice - a more bearish reading than the rubric-1 classification

items.label: BNPL delinquency trend (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 spiking)
items.rationale: Affirm 30+ DPD is flat YoY at 2.8% (not up >100 bps), Klarna delinquency metrics are declining YoY/QoQ, and industry charge-offs remain well below 3%—squarely within the STABLE rubric (flat or down YoY, charge-offs contained). No named provider meets the RISING or SPIKING thresholds. [vintage guard: new read is 2026-Q1/Q2 data but the prior applied value was 2026-08-27 data; kept the newer vintage]
items.fact: Affirm 30+ DPD held flat at 2.8% YoY in Q1 FY2026 (quarter ended March 31, 2026), per its shareholder letter; Klarna Pay Later 30+ DPD fell to 1.3% in Q1 2026 (down 30 bps QoQ) and POS installment 30+ DPD at 3.0% (down 20 bps), per Klarna Q2 2026 slides (Investing.com, ~Aug 2026). Richmond Fed (Feb 2026) cites industry charge-off rate of 1.83% for 2023, falling, with 'no clear evidence of elevated stress.'

dissent.view: LendingTree March 2026 survey finds 47% of BNPL users self-reported a late payment in the past year, up from 41% in 2025—suggesting rising consumer strain not yet captured in hard delinquency series.

items.label: CMBS office delinquency rate (%)
items.rationale: The rubric requires the latest Trepp CMBS office delinquency percent; the most recent explicitly stated Trepp office figure found is 12.34% (January 2026). KBRA data (a dissenting source) shows the office rate at 13.9% in January 2026 and 12.8% in February 2026, suggesting Trepp and KBRA differ by methodology/universe, so the Trepp figure is used as the primary reading. [vintage guard: new read is 2026-01 data but the prior applied value was 2026-03 data; kept the newer vintage]
items.fact: The Trepp CMBS office delinquency rate rose 103 basis points to an all-time high of 12.34 percent in January 2026, per Multi-Housing News citing Trepp data (published ~Feb 2026). The overall Trepp CMBS rate was 7.86% in July 2026 (the latest available month), but no Trepp office-sector-specific figure beyond January 2026 was retrievable from public sources.

dissent.view: KBRA-rated CMBS office delinquency rate was 13.9% in January 2026, falling to 12.8% in February 2026 — higher than Trepp's 12.34% for the same period, reflecting a different rated universe and methodology.
S&P Global noted the CMBS office rate 'surpasses 10.5%' in January 2026 (paywalled headline figure, lower bound only).

items.label: Catastrophe-loss pressure (0 normal / 1 elevated / 2 severe season)
items.rationale: YTD insured losses ($42-47bn) are materially below the 10-year H1 average ($64-66bn), satisfying neither the '>average' trigger for level 1 nor the '>150% of average' or '>$30bn single event' thresholds for level 2; no single event breached the $10bn threshold required for even level 1.
items.fact: Swiss Re Institute reports global insured nat-cat losses of $42bn in H1 2026, 16% below the $66bn long-term H1 trend; Gallagher Re puts H1 at $46bn, 28% below its $64bn 10-year average; no single event exceeded $5bn insured in H1 2026 (Swiss Re / Gallagher Re / Aon, July 2026). No major hurricane landfall or >$10bn single event reported through early September 2026.

dissent.view: Aon estimates H1 2026 at $47bn (vs Swiss Re $42bn and Gallagher Re $46bn) - all still below average, direction consistent
Munich Re pegs H1 2026 at $44bn, also below long-term averages

items.label: GPU-backed debt refinancing stress (0 none / 1 signs / 2 acute)
items.rationale: CoreWeave is a named borrower facing a demonstrated refinancing wall (had to sweeten a $2.6B deal) with CDS pricing at distressed levels, and major banks are offloading AI/data-center debt -- all squarely matching Rubric 1 SIGNS criteria. No confirmed outright default or distressed exchange has been reported, so Rubric 2 ACUTE is not warranted.
items.fact: On July 29 2026, CoreWeave (CRWV) CDS spread hit ~855 bps (implied ~50% five-year default probability); within days CoreWeave had to sweeten terms to place a $2.6B leveraged loan tied to its Anthropic relationship -- per Metir AI (Aug 2 2026) and TechTimes (Jul 30 2026). Separately, JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley and SMBC were actively seeking to offload AI data-center debt via Significant Risk Transfers (SRTs), per FT/Tech Newsday May 3-6 2026.

dissent.view: CoreWeave closed an $8.5B investment-grade-rated GPU-backed DDTL 4.0 facility (A3/Moody's, A-low/DBRS) on March 31 2026 and Q1 2026 revenue of $2.078B beat consensus by >5%, suggesting the primary market remained open to well-structured GPU-backed paper at near-investment-grade spreads.

items.label: Regional-bank CRE stress (0 calm / 1 isolated / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: The rubric's ISOLATED threshold (score=1) is satisfied by at least one public FDIC enforcement action in the trailing 6 months (April 2026 action preceding Community Bank and Trust - West Georgia closure) and 1-2 small-bank failures with documented or inferred CRE/real-estate exposure, each well below $10bn in assets. The CLUSTER threshold (score=2) is not met because explicit CRE attribution by regulators is confirmed for fewer than 3 failures and no single failure exceeded $10bn assets nor was a coordinated interagency emergency action identified.
items.fact: Forbes Advisor (updated ~Aug 2026, drawing on FDIC data last refreshed Aug 21 2026) reports five US bank failures YTD 2026, including Community Bank and Trust - West Georgia (closed May 1 2026, <$10bn assets) which followed an FDIC enforcement action issued April 2026, and Metropolitan Capital Bank & Trust (Jan 30 2026, $261M assets) which Bisnow documented had real-estate/CRE-linked loan exposure. At least 3-4 failures fall in the trailing 6-month window (Mar-Sep 2026), but explicit FDIC/Fed/OCC attribution of CRE concentration as a stated cause is confirmed for only 1-2 of those failures; no single failure exceeded $10bn assets and no coordinated interagency emergency facility was identified. Sources: https://www.forbes.com/advisor/banking/list-of-failed-banks/ ; https://www.fdic.gov/bank-failures/failed-bank-list (Aug 21 2026); https://www.bisnow.com/national/news/capital-markets/cre-tied-to-first-bank-failure-of-2026-133023

dissent.view: Bankrate (as of Feb 2026) reported only 1 bank failure in 2026 (Metropolitan Capital), suggesting lower failure count if their data was not updated to reflect subsequent 2026 closures - however Forbes and FDIC data supersede this as more current.

items.label: Subprime auto 60+ day delinquency (%)
items.rationale: The Fitch Auto ABS Index is the primary institutional benchmark for subprime auto 60+ DPD; the June 2026 reading of 5.67% is the latest hard monthly figure available, representing a seasonal improvement from the January record but still materially elevated vs. historical norms. The rubric calls for the latest reported percent, which maps directly to 5.67.
items.fact: Fitch Ratings subprime auto ABS 60+ day delinquency rate in June 2026 was 5.67%, down 64 bps year-over-year (Wolf Street, August 13 2026, citing Fitch Auto ABS Index). Peak was 6.90% in January 2026.

dissent.view: Motley Fool (Sep 2, 2026) citing Fitch places Q2-end subprime at ~5.8% and notes July showed 'renewed deterioration,' implying the rate may have risen above 5.67% in July-August 2026 — but no hard July/August monthly figure was publicly confirmed.

Symend (updated Aug 31, 2026) and multiple sources anchor the January 2026 peak at 6.9% per Fitch, with narrative that Q2 improved but H2 2026 expected to re-weaken; no single competing monthly number for July-August confirmed.

items.label: Large public-pension funded ratio (%)
items.rationale: The rubric requests a representative large US public-pension funded ratio as a percent; the Milliman PPFI is the standard monthly benchmark for the 100 largest plans and its July 31, 2026 reading of 88.2% is the most recently published authoritative figure, mapping directly to the rubric's requested metric.
items.fact: Milliman 100 Public Pension Funding Index (PPFI): funded ratio of the 100 largest U.S. public pension plans was 88.2% as of July 31, 2026, down from 88.7% as of June 30, 2026. Source: Milliman / BusinessWire, published August 27, 2026 (https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260827829119/en/Milliman-analysis-Public-pension-funded-ratio-slips-again-to-88.2-as-of-July-31).

dissent.view: Equable Institute 'State of Pensions 2026' projects the national average funded ratio (253 statewide and municipal systems) at 85.0% for FY2026, up from 81.2% in FY2025 — a broader universe than the Milliman top-100 and based on actuarial (not market) valuation dates.

S&P Global Ratings (Jan 2026) estimated a sustainable funded ratio of ~81% for typical public-pension issuers based on FY2025 audit data (June 30, 2025 measurement), reflecting a longer actuarial lag.

items.label: New IMF programs / missed coupons (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: One sovereign (Ethiopia) is in confirmed active default/restructuring within or persisting into the trailing 6-month window; Bangladesh's program request is talk not action (no Board approval confirmed). One active distress event maps to RISING (band 1: 1-2 events).
items.fact: Ethiopia remains in active default on its $1B Eurobond (original missed coupon Dec 2023); on June 29 2026 an agreement-in-principle with ~45% of holders was announced but the exchange is not yet executed (africasacountry.com, July 14 2026). Bangladesh formally requested a new IMF arrangement on June 3 2026 (imf.org/en/news/articles/2026/06/03), but Board approval has not been confirmed. Pakistan's May 8 2026 IMF action was a 3rd-review disbursement under its existing EFF, not a new program (imf.org, May 8 2026). No additional new missed coupons or Board-approved new EM programs confirmed in the March-September 2026 window.

dissent.view: Bangladesh's June 3 2026 formal IMF request could be counted as a new program initiation if the Board approves during the window, which would push the count toward 2 events, still RISING

items.label: Reserve-weaponization / settlement shift (0 none / 1 talk / 2 action)
items.rationale: No new sovereign reserve seizure (ownership transfer) has been executed in 2026—the Russian freeze pre-dates the rubric window and full confiscation was explicitly rejected in Dec 2025, ruling out score 2. BRICS Pay operational deployment and 'The Unit' sandbox constitute new non-dollar settlement system launches/agreements with official backing, placing the indicator firmly at score 1 (TALK/early launch).
items.fact: As of April 2026 (IAI Brief 26|17, April 2026): EU chose 'joint borrowing over confiscation in December 2025,' leaving Russian sovereign assets (~€210bn) frozen but NOT seized. items.label: Social Security / pension reform shock (0 none / 1 debate / 2 cuts)
items.rationale: The trustees report materially worsened the OASI depletion date (2033 -> 2032) and widened the long-run funding gap, and reform is actively debated in Congress -- both conditions for band 1 (DEBATE). No automatic reduction has been triggered (depletion is still 6 years away) and no legislation enacting cuts has been signed into law, ruling out band 2 (CUTS).
items.fact: The 2026 Social Security Trustees Report (released June 9, 2026, SSA.gov/oact) projects the OASI Trust Fund depleted in Q4 2032 -- one quarter earlier than the 2025 report -- with the 75-year actuarial deficit widening to 4.42% of taxable payroll (up 16% from 3.82%). Multiple reform bills are actively debated in Congress (e.g., Bipartisan Social Security Commission Act H.R. 9187; PROMISE Act introduced July 14, 2026) but NO benefit cuts have been enacted or automatically triggered.

dissent.view: CBO (Feb 2026) estimates the automatic cut upon 2032 depletion at ~28%, vs. the Trustees' 22%, reflecting different economic assumptions -- same depletion date but larger projected shortfall

items.label: USD share of FX reserves (%, IMF COFER)

items.label: Export-control escalation (0 stable / 1 tightening / 2 retaliation)
items.rationale: Both the US/allied side (Entity List additions, MATCH Act pressure, ASML circumvention accusations) and China (MOFCOM Announcement No. 30, August 5 countermeasure package, 50% domestic procurement mandate) enacted new active measures within the trailing 3 months; China's MOFCOM actions constitute explicit counter-controls against US and allied entities, satisfying the rubric's level-2 threshold of target-country countermeasures.
items.fact: In the trailing 3 months: (1) US/allied side — MATCH Act debated in Congress (would blanket-ban all ASML immersion DUV exports to China), BIS added 52 Chinese entities to Entity List (July 2026, CNC/adjacent-tech category), US Commerce Secretary accused ASML of circumventing controls (June 2026). dissent.view: The Busan truce (Oct 2025) suspended the BIS Affiliates Rule and China's Oct 9 extraterritorial measures through Nov 2026, and BIS Entity List additions in July 2026 clustered in CNC/adjacent categories rather than core semiconductor SME — suggesting the semiconductor-specific escalation track remains partially restrained by the truce framework. This could support a read of level 1 (tightening) rather than full level 2 retaliation specifically on semiconductors.

items.label: Hormuz/Red Sea status (0 open / 1 contested / 2 closed)
items.rationale: At ~7% of pre-crisis transit volume with active Iranian military strikes on commercial vessels, no operational convoy regime, and Brent at ~$97/bbl (~47% above year-prior levels), all three rubric conditions for a '2=CLOSED' rating are met: volume well below 25% of normal, no convoy workaround, and a corroborating oil price signal consistent with closure.

items.label: New tariff/anti-dumping actions (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 escalating)

items.label: Nov-2025 pause status (0 extended / 1 expiring / 2 lapsed)
items.rationale: Both rubric-1 triggers are met: (a) fewer than 90 days remain to the Nov 10, 2026 nominal expiry with no announced renewal, and (b) China's June 22, 2026 entity-list additions of MP Materials and USA Rare Earth constitute a partial breach. Score 2 is not warranted because the broad suspension is still formally operative and market signals (muted equity reaction, analysts calling the listings 'largely symbolic') do not corroborate full collapse.
items.fact: The Nov-2025 US-China minerals truce (China's suspension of Oct-9-2025 rare earth export controls) remains formally in force until Nov 10, 2026 per MOFCOM Announcements 55-62 (Nov 7, 2025) and White House Fact Sheet (Nov 5, 2025). dissent.view: FDD (June 24, 2026) argues the June 22 entity-list action 'ended the pause,' implying Score 2 (lapsed/controls reimposed); but this reads entity-specific dual-use restrictions as equivalent to full reimposition of broad export controls, which market prices and the formal MOFCOM suspension status do not support.

items.label: Rare-earth export license flow (0 flowing / 1 slowing / 2 frozen)
items.rationale: The regime is case-by-case licensing for most exporters (general licences cover only a whitelist of three named producers), processing times far exceed 30 days (60–120 days reported), and new categories (samarium, gadolinium, lutetium) were added to the control list in the trailing three months relative to the as-of date — all of which maps squarely to rubric level 1 (SLOWING). [cross-check (asi1): two reads disagreed (1 vs 0); held for review]
items.fact: China's core April 2025 rare-earth export licensing regime (covering seven medium/heavy REEs and downstream magnets containing Tb/Dy) remains fully in force under MOFCOM case-by-case licensing. General licences were issued in December 2025 to a handful of pre-cleared Chinese exporters (JL MAG, San Huan, Yunsheng) but are 'not broadly available.' Processing times run 45 working days by statute but 'routinely exceed 60–120 days' in practice for heavy-REE approvals. Sources: blog.gettransport.com (July 7, 2026); rare-earth-mining.com (April 2026); certivo.com (March 2026); techtimes.com (May 27, 2026).

dissent.view: Multi-institutional analysis cited by Rare Earth Exchanges reports licensing approval rates below 25% for European firms, implying near-categorical denial for some buyer segments — a potential level-2 read for EU-destination shipments.

items.label: Single-point concentration (0 easing / 1 high / 2 extreme)

The Arizona and Kumamoto 3nm fabs are real but future-dated (2027-2028), so no market volume signal supports any current overseas share.
items.fact: As of September 2026, all TSMC leading-edge (<=3nm) capacity is 100% in Taiwan: 3nm at ~180,000 wpm and 2nm ramping to ~100,000 wpm, both exclusively at Taiwan fabs (Fab 18, Fab 20, Fab 22). TSMC long-term plan targets ~30% of advanced output in the US across six Arizona fabs, framing current concentration as transitional rather than structural

items.label: Taiwan / cross-strait tension (0 calm / 1 elevated / 2 crisis)
items.rationale: Persistent record-high PRC vessel presence and a recent live-fire drill in the Strait qualify as assertive/elevated pressure (Rubric 1), but there is no kinetic clash, formal blockade, or full mobilization signal, so Rubric 2 is not met.

items.label: AI power-demand pressure (0 easing / 1 tight / 2 acute)
items.rationale: Three confirmed DOE 202(c) emergency orders in 2026 authorizing curtailment of data-center load on PJM and ERCOT, plus statewide moratoriums in New York and Texas, satisfy the rubric's top band: confirmed curtailment authority exercised and power-scarcity-driven moratoria declared. items.rationale: Three or more named top-20 mines (Grasberg, Kamoa-Kakula, Caserones) have confirmed active, measured production cuts in 2026, and institutions including Benchmark Minerals and ICSG have forecast a market deficit partly attributable to these disruptions — this maps squarely to rubric level 2 (CLUSTER: >=3 major mines disrupted, OR lost output large enough that institutions forecast a market deficit).

The ICSG cut its 2026 mine supply growth forecast to 1.6% from 2.3% citing DRC, Chile and Indonesia constraints including Grasberg and Kamoa (Oregon Group, May 2026), and Benchmark Minerals forecast a refined copper market deficit in 2026 due to Grasberg alone.

items.label: Insurer non-renewals / exits (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 accelerating)
items.rationale: Documented non-renewal waves span approximately 13 states across all NAIC regions, placing this squarely in the 5-15 state RISING band; the rubric threshold for ACCELERATING (>15 states or full top-10 insurer exit) is not clearly met, and NAIC's own characterisation of broad market operational strength plus FL stabilisation signals keep this out of the most severe tier.
items.fact: NAIC Aug 5 2026 report ('Examining Homeowner Property Insurance Market Dynamics', MCAS 2018-2024) finds company-initiated non-renewal rates rose 96%-216% across ALL regional zones; Climate Cosmos (Jun 2026) enumerates 13 named states with active non-renewal/exit waves (CA, FL, LA, TX, GA, OK, CO and others); FL non-renewed 3.35% of policies (highest nationally), CA 3.18% (3.9x 2018 rate); NAIC simultaneously characterises the market as 'operationally strong overall' with improved 2024 underwriting and 715 active carriers; FL Citizens count fell to ~385K-395K by Jan 2026 (lowest since 2012), a partial stabilisation signal. No confirmed full exit by a top-10 insurer from a major state in 2026. Sources: content.naic.org Aug 5 2026; climatecosmos.com Jun 18 2026; leadgen-economy.com Jun 25 2026.

items.label: Govt stability (0 stable / 1 fragile / 2 collapse-or-snap-election)
items.rationale: The government holds no working majority and has repeatedly invoked Article 49.3 while surviving — not losing — multiple no-confidence votes; this maps precisely to Rubric Band 1 (FRAGILE). Band 2 is excluded because no confidence vote was passed and no dissolution or snap election was called.
items.fact: The Second Lecornu government (minority coalition: RE, MoDem, HOR, UDI) is incumbent since 10 Oct 2025. It invoked Article 49.3 to pass both the revenue and expenditure sections of the 2026 budget, surviving four separate no-confidence motions in Jan 2026 (highest tally: 269 vs. 288 required on 23 Jan 2026). Budget adopted 2 Feb 2026 after two further failed motions (260 vs. 289 required). Sources: Euronews 23 Jan 2026 (https://www.euronews.com/2026/01/23/french-government-avoids-collapse-after-surviving-two-no-confidence-votes), Al Jazeera 2 Feb 2026 (https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/2/2/france-adopts-2026-budget-after-two-no-confidence-votes-fail), Wikipedia Second Lecornu government (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Lecornu_government).

items.label: Pension-fund leverage event, UK-2022 type (0 none / 1 stress / 2 blowup)
items.rationale: Rubric level 0 requires LDI buffers adequate with no margin stress cited by TPR/ESMA. TPR's own market-oversight data confirm buffers at ~300 bps (above the 250 bps regulatory minimum), leverage materially reduced, and no forced-selling or regulator-flagged liquidity crisis in 2025-2026; the Jan-2025 gilt selloff produced orderly cash calls, not a blowup. No evidence of a 2026 episode elevating this to level 1 or 2.
items.fact: TPR market oversight report (data to 31 March 2025) states: the LDI market has shrunk from ~£1.5 trillion (end-2021) to ~£0.7 trillion; daily volatility in leveraged LDI assets is more than 50% lower than at end-2021; LDI managers have raised rate buffers to ~300 bps (vs ~150 bps pre-2022); and 'LDI managers have maintained higher buffer thresholds, reducing leverage and improved collateral management.' No regulator alert, forced-selling episode, or central-bank intervention has been identified in 2026. Source: TPR, 'Market Oversight: How well pension schemes are prepared for LDI risk', thepensionsregulator.gov.uk (data to 31 March 2025). The most recent gilt-yield stress episode (Jan 2025, 30-yr gilt at 26-yr high) saw some cash calls but market advisers described it as 'orderly' with no forced selling — Reuters/MarketScreener, January 2025.

items.label: Rating action (0 stable / 1 negative outlook / 2 downgrade)
items.rationale: Rubric band 2 requires an actual rating cut in the trailing 12 months; both Fitch (Sep 2025) and S&P (Oct 17 2025) executed one-notch cuts from AA- to A+, each within 12 months of 2026-09-07. Moody's negative outlook (band 1) is also present but is subordinate to the confirmed downgrades.
items.fact: Fitch cut France from AA- to A+ (stable outlook) in September 2025; S&P cut France from AA- to A+ (stable outlook) on 17 October 2025 (spglobal.com, france24.com); Moody's kept Aa3 but revised outlook to negative on 25 October 2025 (france24.com). Both Fitch and S&P downgrades are within the trailing 12 months. As of late August 2026 Fitch reaffirmed A+/stable and S&P reaffirmed A+/stable in May 2026; Moody's Aa3/negative remains in force.

items.label: China PPI YoY (%) - large swing either way is worse
items.rationale: At +3.5% YoY, China PPI is in positive territory and represents a meaningful cost-push signal after a prolonged deflationary streak that ended in March 2026; the rubric scores on the SIZE of the move, and +3.5% is a moderate positive print flagging input-cost pressure exportable to global supply chains.
items.fact: China PPI for industrial products increased by 3.5% year on year in July 2026, per NBS official English press release (stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202608/t20260810_1965017.html), released 2026-08-10. Corroborated by Xinhua (2026-08-09) and SCIO (2026-08-10). August 2026 data not yet published (NBS typically releases ~10th of following month; today is 2026-09-07).

items.label: Ex-China heavy rare-earth price premium (x China)
items.rationale: Triangulating the most recent official Chinese price data (CTIA Aug 2026) against contemporaneous ex-China assessments (REEx Sept 2026, Argus/Reuters June 2026) yields a central ex-China HREE premium multiple of ~4-5x; 4.5 is the midpoint of the Argus x4-x5 range and consistent with the REEx 'up to 4x' floor, mapped directly to the rubric's multiple format.
items.fact: Rare Earth Exchanges (Sept 3 2026, anchored to Aug 2026 CREIA data) states dysprosium and terbium cost 'up to 4x more outside China'; Argus data cited by Reuters (June 2026) puts the ex-China premium for dysprosium and terbium oxide at 'x4 to x5'; CTIA Aug 2026 official China avg: terbium oxide RMB 6,680/kg (~$920/kg), dysprosium oxide RMB 1,423/kg (~$196/kg); Platts CIF North America (Mar 31 2026): terbium $4,900/kg (~5.3x), dysprosium $1,200/kg (~6.3x); Benchmark Minerals (Mar 24 2026): 2025 avg dysprosium CIF North America was 4.4x EXW China.

items.label: US domestic RE producer blacklist (0 none / 1 entity-specific ban / 2 sector-wide ban)
items.rationale: Two named US rare-earth producers (MP Materials, USA Rare Earth) are on the MOFCOM export-control list as of 22 June 2026, satisfying rubric level 1 (entity-specific). Multiple sources explicitly confirm the restriction is firm-specific and does not constitute a blanket/sector-wide ban on US rare-earth producers as a class, ruling out level 2.
items.fact: MOFCOM Announcement No. 23 of 2026 (issued 22 June 2026, effective immediately) named 10 specific US entities on China's export control list. The two US rare-earth producers explicitly listed are MP Materials Corp. and USA Rare Earth, Inc. The full list: Aveox, Red Cat Holdings, Teal Drones, IMSAR, Jaia Robotics, Ball Aerospace & Technologies Corp, Oshkosh Defense, L3Harris Maritime Services, MP Materials Corp, and USA Rare Earth. The measure bans dual-use item exports to the named firms only. Multiple corroborating sources (Global Times citing MOFCOM directly, Bloomberg, Reuters via Al Jazeera, Benchmark Minerals, Arnold & Porter legal advisory) confirm the restriction is entity-specific. Market signal: MP Materials stock was roughly flat on announcement day and USA Rare Earth was modestly higher — consistent with a firm-specific, partially symbolic action rather than a sector-wide shock. Primary source: MOFCOM Announcement No. 23 of 2026, https://english.mofcom.gov.cn; corroborated by https://www.globaltimes.cn/page/202606/1364081.shtml and https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-06-22/china-places-two-us-rare-earths-producers-on-export-control-list

items.label: Food-price trend (0 falling / 1 elevated / 2 spiking)
items.rationale: MoM gain of +1.9% is below the 5% SPIKING threshold; the 3-month rise (June 130.3 to August 133.3) is ~2.3%, well below the 10% SPIKING threshold; index is rising both MoM and YoY, placing it squarely in ELEVATED (1).
items.fact: FAO Food Price Index averaged 133.3 points in August 2026, up 1.9% from revised July level (131.1) and 2.5% from a year ago, reaching its highest level since end-2022. Source: FAO newsroom, https://www.fao.org/newsroom/detail/supply-concerns-drive-fao-food-price-index-higher/en, released 4 September 2026.

flags.name: Redemption gates widespread, but HY spreads benign
flags.message: Large-fund redemption gates are rated WIDESPREAD (2) but high-yield spreads are benign. Broad gating usually coincides with visible credit stress; confirm the gates are systemic, not a couple of isolated funds.

s1_basis_trade.label: Hidden leverage in US government bonds
s1_basis_trade.gist: Hedge funds borrow heavily to trade US government bonds; if that trade unwinds fast it can freeze the market everyone treats as safe.

s2_japan.label: Japan's rates and the global cash carry trade
s2_japan.gist: Cheap Japanese money has funded bets worldwide for years; as Japan's interest rates rise, pulling that money home can ripple through global markets.

s3_private_credit.label: Private lending you can't see into
s3_private_credit.gist: A fast-growing pile of loans sits outside the banks with little public disclosure, so stress there is hard to spot until it is already large.

s4_dev_debt.label: Debt stress in developing countries
s4_dev_debt.gist: Many poorer nations owe more than they can comfortably repay; a wave of defaults can spread and pull in their lenders.

s5_china_deflation.label: China's prices spilling into the world
s5_china_deflation.gist: Big swings in China's factory prices - falling or rising - get exported to everyone else as cheaper goods or higher input costs.

s6_rare_earths.label: Rare-earth minerals used as a weapon
s6_rare_earths.gist: China controls most of the world's rare-earth processing and is now restricting it, squeezing US defense and high-tech manufacturing.

s7_stablecoins.label: Crypto dollars and US government debt
s7_stablecoins.gist: Stablecoins must hold US Treasuries as backing, so their rapid growth - or a sudden wobble - now feeds straight back into the government-debt market.

s8_ai_capex.label: The AI spending boom
s8_ai_capex.gist: Enormous borrowing to build AI data centers is racing ahead of the revenue meant to justify it, concentrating the risk in a few giant companies.

s9_cre.label: Commercial real estate and small banks
s9_cre.gist: Half-empty offices and loans coming due strain the regional banks that hold them - a slow-burning credit risk.

s10_france.label: France and eurozone stability
s10_france.gist: A politically gridlocked, heavily indebted France is the soft spot that could reopen broader euro-area stress.

s11_consumer_debt.label: Household debt strain
s11_consumer_debt.gist: Rising late payments on car loans and buy-now-pay-later show households stretching - an early warning on consumer health.

s12_gold_dedollar.label: Gold and moving away from the dollar
s12_gold_dedollar.gist: Central banks stockpiling gold and building non-dollar payment systems slowly chip away at the dollar's dominance.

s13_insurance.label: Insurers pulling back
s13_insurance.gist: As disaster losses climb, insurers raise prices or quit whole regions, leaving homes and assets exposed.

s14_pensions.label: Pensions and an aging population
s14_pensions.gist: Aging populations and underfunded pensions strain public budgets; leveraged pension funds can also break in a sudden rate shock, as the UK saw in 2022.

s15_ai_power.label: AI's strain on the power grid
s15_ai_power.gist: AI data centers need more electricity than the grid can quickly supply, triggering curtailments, building moratoria, and multi-year connection queues.

s16_copper.label: Copper for electrification
s16_copper.gist: Electrifying everything needs far more copper than mines can deliver, and major mine outages are tightening supply further.

s17_water.label: Water as a hidden constraint
s17_water.gist: Droughts and shrinking reservoirs threaten chip factories, farms, and power generation - an underpriced input with no substitute.

s18_food_fertilizer.label: Food and fertilizer supply
s18_food_fertilizer.gist: Export curbs and shipping disruptions to fertilizer raise the risk of higher food prices down the line.

s19_lithography.label: The chipmaking chokepoint
s19_lithography.gist: The most advanced chips depend on one Dutch tool-maker and Taiwan's factories; any disruption there hits the entire tech economy.

s20_sea_lanes.label: Shipping lanes and undersea cables
s20_sea_lanes.gist: Key straits like Hormuz and the undersea cables carrying the internet are vulnerable chokepoints for global trade and data.

s21_clearinghouses.label: The financial system's plumbing
s21_clearinghouses.gist: Clearinghouses sit at the center of every market; if one seized up under stress, it would jam trading everywhere at once.

playbook.disclaimer: Educational cause-and-effect only - how stress like this has historically moved through the system. Nothing here is investment advice or a prediction.

s1_basis_trade.mechanism: A rates shock forces highly leveraged government-bond arbitrage positions to unwind at once: margin calls trigger forced Treasury selling, liquidity in the world's benchmark market evaporates, and everything priced off it reprices.
benefits: cash and short-term bills through the panic
long-term government bonds AFTER central-bank intervention
s1_basis_trade.watch: The funding-spread and bond-volatility rows above; the historical pivot was the central bank announcing a backstop facility.
s1_basis_trade.trap: In past episodes the 'safe' asset itself fell first - forced sellers sell what they can - so the flight-to-safety instinct lost money until the intervention.

s2_japan.mechanism: Surging Japanese yields pull decades of cheap yen funding home: the yen spikes on repatriation, and leveraged positions worldwide that were financed in yen get liquidated together - hitting high-momentum equities and emerging markets hardest.
benefits: Japanese banks and insurers as rates normalize
s2_japan.watch: The 30-year JGB row above (live official feed) and the yen; past unwinds announced themselves through the currency.
s2_japan.trap: Historical carry unwinds were violent but brief - the 2024 episode round-tripped within days; the durable shift was in Japanese financials, not the panic.

s3_private_credit.mechanism: One honest markdown forces everyone's marks: investor withdrawals hit gates, gated funds fire-sell into an illiquid market, and lending to mid-sized companies contracts just as they need to refinance.
bleeds: private-credit vehicles trading below stated asset value
benefits: holders of dry powder buying discounted credit afterwards
public high-quality credit as the flight destination
s3_private_credit.watch: The default-rate and redemption-gate rows above; public high-yield spreads are the honest proxy for hidden marks.
s3_private_credit.trap: Opacity means the repricing arrives as a sudden gap, not a trend - by the time it is public, the move has largely happened.

s4_dev_debt.mechanism: A cluster of sovereign defaults - not one - overwhelms the restructuring machinery: redemptions from emerging-market debt funds force indiscriminate selling of strong and weak credits alike, and stress spreads through common creditors.
benefits: and historically the buyers of defaulted debt after restructuring - among the best-documented recoveries in fixed income
s4_dev_debt.watch: The new-IMF-programs row above and the dollar's strength, which is usually the upstream cause.
s4_dev_debt.trap: Index diversification means one or two defaults barely register; the systemic wave this story warns of is exactly what official bailouts exist to prevent.

s5_china_deflation.mechanism: Deepening factory-gate deflation is exported as cheaper goods, compressing margins for competing producers everywhere - unless Beijing's stimulus response whipsaws the pressure into a sudden commodity and China-equity rebound.
benefits: long-term bonds in the deflation leg
Chinese equities and industrial metals in the stimulus leg
s5_china_deflation.watch: The producer-price row above and any stimulus announcement - the two legs point opposite directions.
s5_china_deflation.trap: Policy whipsaw: historically every stimulus rumor violently reversed the deflation trade within days.

s6_rare_earths.mechanism: Export restrictions tighten into denial: magnet and heavy-rare-earth supply to defense, vehicle, and robotics manufacturers halts, panic stockpiling begins, and processing capacity outside China re-rates from commodity business to strategic asset.
bleeds: vehicle and defense production schedules in the short run
s6_rare_earths.watch: The license-flow, blacklist, and ex-China premium rows above - the premium is the market's own severity gauge.
s6_rare_earths.trap: Historically these moves reversed as fast as they started on any truce headline, and diversified funds in the space often hold the Chinese producers too.

s7_stablecoins.mechanism: A run on a major stablecoin forces its reserves - tens of billions in short-term government debt - to liquidate within days, briefly dislocating the bill market while the crypto ecosystem's dollar rails seize and leveraged positions cascade.
benefits: historically the surviving issuer gained lasting market share after each depeg scare
s7_stablecoins.watch: The live peg-deviation and supply rows above (updated daily from the aggregator) - past runs announced themselves in the peg first.
s7_stablecoins.trap: Crypto markets have a long history of face-ripping rebounds inside downtrends; past episodes punished conviction in both directions.

s8_ai_capex.mechanism: The debt-financed buildout meets a revenue shortfall: one credit event at a leveraged data-center operator reprices all AI-adjacent borrowing, capital-spending guidance gets cut, chip orders fall, and power-demand forecasts deflate - the whole complex moves together because it was funded together.
bleeds: power producers priced on AI demand
benefits: and - the dot-com lesson - the post-bust survivors compounded for a decade
s8_ai_capex.watch: The capex-gap, revenue-gap, and refinancing rows above; credit stress historically led equity repricing.
s8_ai_capex.trap: Bubbles run longer than solvency: betting against this one early has been the era's classic ruin trade, which is why timing signals matter more than valuation.

s9_cre.mechanism: Office refinancing failures cluster into bank failures: deposit flight spreads to lookalike regional lenders, credit to small business contracts, and commercial-property marks finally reflect reality.
benefits: the largest banks via deposit inflows
and historically the whole sector rebounded within days of a backstop
s9_cre.watch: The bank-failure and office-delinquency rows above and the official problem-bank list.
s9_cre.trap: The 2023 backstop bottomed the sector in 48 hours - the policy response, not the failure, was the historical turning point.

s10_france.mechanism: Fiscal paralysis pushes French borrowing costs through crisis thresholds: banks holding the government's own bonds absorb the losses, the sovereign-bank doom loop reawakens, and stress spreads across euro-area borrowing costs.
bleeds: other high-debt euro members through contagion
benefits: and non-euro safe havens in every euro crisis
s10_france.watch: The OAT-Bund spread row above (live feed) - it is the market's single-number verdict on this story.
s10_france.trap: The central bank: euro-breakup positioning has been ruined repeatedly by ECB backstops built precisely for this scenario.

s11_consumer_debt.mechanism: Subprime stress spreads upward: rising late payments become charge-offs, lenders tighten, discretionary spending cracks, and the weakness travels from consumer lenders to retailers to the broad economy.
benefits: trade-down retailers in every past consumer squeeze
s11_consumer_debt.watch: The subprime-delinquency and BNPL rows above; the staples-versus-discretionary ratio is the market's own recession gauge.
s11_consumer_debt.trap: Lenders provision ahead of losses - their shares historically bottomed while delinquencies were still rising.

s12_gold_dedollar.mechanism: A reserve-weaponization event accelerates the slow shift: central banks swap dollar assets for gold at a faster pace, marginal foreign demand for government debt weakens, and the metal gains a structural, price-insensitive buyer.
bleeds: long-term government bonds via lost foreign demand
benefits: gold above all - the current central-bank buying era is the live example - plus non-dollar safe havens
s12_gold_dedollar.watch: The reserve-share row above (quarterly official data) and central-bank purchase reports.
s12_gold_dedollar.trap: This is measured in decades, not events - and gold miners have historically lagged the metal itself across full cycles.

s13_insurance.mechanism: A mega-catastrophe season collides with insurers already exiting exposed regions: property becomes uninsurable, collateral values fall, and the stress transmits to mortgages, regional lenders, and state backstops.
bleeds: property values and lenders in exposed regions
benefits: historically reinsurers AFTER the event as pricing hardened
and catastrophe-linked debt yields for risk-bearers
s13_insurance.watch: The insurer-exit and catastrophe-loss rows above plus the season's forecasts.
s13_insurance.trap: Positioning before the event absorbs the loss; the well-documented historical pattern favored the post-event hard market.

s14_pensions.mechanism: A rate spike forces leveraged pension strategies into collateral calls: they dump whatever is liquid, the selling pushes yields higher still, and the spiral continues until a central bank steps in - the UK lived this in 2022.
bleeds: long-term government bonds during the spiral itself
retirees' security in the slow version
benefits: whoever provided liquidity at the intervention - the 2022 central-bank entry marked the exact bottom - and retirement insurers structurally as rates rose
s14_pensions.watch: The funded-ratio row above (live monthly feed) and long-bond volatility.
s14_pensions.trap: Identical to the basis trade: buying the falling 'safe' asset before the intervention caught knives for days.

s15_ai_power.mechanism: Data-center demand outruns the grid so badly that curtailments, connection queues, and building moratoria stall the buildout - rising household bills turn it political, and the constraint moves from engineering to consent.
bleeds: utilities caught between regulators and demand
benefits: and nuclear/gas capacity - though see the trap
s15_ai_power.watch: The interconnection-wait and moratoria rows above and capacity-auction prices.
s15_ai_power.trap: The famous version of this trade assumes the buildout CONTINUES; this story's actual blow-up - moratoria stopping it - points the opposite way for the same names.

s16_copper.mechanism: A structural deficit meets a supply shock - a major mine closure removes years of planned supply - and the metal prices high enough to ration demand, raising costs for every grid, vehicle, and data-center project simultaneously.
benefits: producing miners with volume to sell
s16_copper.watch: The mine-disruption and deficit rows above and exchange inventory levels.
s16_copper.trap: The political risk that causes the shocks sits inside the producers themselves - the closed mine may be the one you were counting on.

s17_water.mechanism: Severe drought hits a chip hub, a farm belt, and cooling-dependent power at once: an unpriced input becomes a binding constraint, cutting industrial output regionally and feeding into food prices.
benefits: historically crop prices in drought years
s17_water.watch: The reservoir and drought rows above (live official feed for the largest US reservoir).
s17_water.trap: There is no pure play - broad 'water' funds are mostly global industrials, while the shock is local; the honest effects are second-order.

s18_food_fertilizer.mechanism: Fertilizer export restrictions cut application in poorer countries, next season's yields fall, grain prices spike, and food inflation becomes social and fiscal stress in import-dependent nations - looping back into the developing-world debt story.
benefits: fertilizer producers in every past squeeze
s18_food_fertilizer.watch: The FAO food-price row above (live feed) and the export-curb indicator.
s18_food_fertilizer.trap: Fertilizer stress historically reversed violently when curbs lifted, taking back most of the move.

s19_lithography.mechanism: Conflict or blockade around Taiwan stops the fabs that make nearly all leading-edge chips: every electronics supply chain seizes within a quarter, and the shock is large enough that markets themselves may not function normally.
bleeds: and anything with a chip in it
s19_lithography.watch: The tension and export-control rows above; false-alarm cycles have historically outnumbered real escalations many times over.
s19_lithography.trap: In the true scenario, settlement and market access are themselves at risk - analysis that assumes functioning markets may not apply.

s20_sea_lanes.mechanism: A chokepoint closes - this board just watched Hormuz do it - and shipping rates, war-risk insurance, and energy prices spike together while longer reroutes quietly shrink effective global capacity; cable cuts do the same for data.
s20_sea_lanes.watch: The live strait-transit feed and cable-incident rows above.
s20_sea_lanes.trap: This board's own history shows it: reopening headlines crushed the shipping move within days - persistence of the disruption was everything.

s21_clearinghouses.mechanism: A major member defaults into a volatile market and the clearinghouse's loss waterfall activates: surviving members face assessments and de-risk simultaneously, margin requirements spiral procyclically, and the plumbing everyone assumed away becomes the crisis itself.
benefits: almost nothing leveraged - which is the honest answer; cash
and physical assets have no counterparty
s21_clearinghouses.watch: The clearing-mandate rollout row above and any clearinghouse margin announcements.
s21_clearinghouses.trap: The deepest on the board: in a true clearing failure, a winning derivative position may itself not pay out.

context.intro: The famous dials, for contrast. These are the most-watched macro gauges in the world - shown here so you can compare them with this tracker's structural lens. They are not part of the score. When they disagree with the gauge above, that divergence is the story: markets price these continuously, while the risks this tracker follows are the kind markets historically ignored until they ruptured.

items.label: VIX
items.note: Expected US stock-market volatility - the most-watched fear gauge. Calm markets usually sit below ~20.

items.label: 10y-2y curve
items.note: 10-year minus 2-year Treasury yield. A negative (inverted) reading has historically preceded US recessions - with long and variable lags.

items.label: High-yield spread
items.note: The extra yield markets demand to lend to risky companies - the market's own price of credit stress. Calm is roughly below ~4.

items.label: Chicago Fed NFCI
items.note: The Chicago Fed's broad financial-conditions index across money, debt, and equity markets. Negative = looser (calmer) than average.

items.label: Unemployment
items.note: The US unemployment rate - the classic real-economy dial, updated monthly.
